title: No effort is lost
hookLine: Arjuna asks what happens to someone who starts the path and drifts off it, and Krishna answers
carry: no effort on the path is lost, even across lives

lines: MY MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.
WHAT IF I DRIFT OFF THE PATH?
cards: In the sixth chapter of the Gita, Krishna has been describing the steady yogi, the one who sits still and sees the same Self in every being. And Arjuna, honest as ever, says: my mind is restless, Krishna.
Holding it is like trying to hold the wind. Then he asks the question every beginner asks. What about the one who has faith, who starts, and whose mind wanders off the path before the end?
Is he lost both ways, like a torn cloud in the sky, nothing here, nothing there?

teach.h: NO ONE WHO DOES GOOD COMES TO A BAD END.
teach.b: Krishna's answer is a much-loved passage. In paraphrase: no, Arjuna. Neither in this world nor the next is that person destroyed; no one who does good comes to a bad end.

After a long stay in good worlds, Krishna says, they're born again into a pure and prosperous home, or even into a family of wise yogis. And there they pick up the understanding they had before, and strive again.
Here's the Hindu teaching underneath, plainly.
Karma: what you do leaves an imprint, and the imprint of practice is kept. And rebirth: in Hindu belief the self goes on through many lives, so a path begun isn't canceled when a body ends.
The Gita says it earlier too, in the second chapter: on this path no effort begun is lost, and even a little of this dharma protects from great fear.
Some teachers read that generously: the half-managed sit, the missed week, the prayer you used to know by heart. Others hear it more strictly, about the yoga Krishna is teaching.

teach.h: NO EFFORT ON THE PATH IS LOST.
teach.b: Either way, it's why a Hindu grandparent might tell a child who forgot the aarti that it isn't gone; it's in you, waiting to be picked up.
Year three ends here: a war, a song, a child, the saints, the teachers, and every sit you managed, kept. Tomorrow year four begins with the goddess.

how: Bhagavad Gita 2.40 and 6.40 are quoted by Hindu teachers to encourage people who are starting a practice or returning to one, as a promise that sincere effort on the path is not wasted.

o: the year just walked and kept, with new ranges beyond it
a finish line after which the path is complete
the year the path begins with the goddess texts

games.q: the beginner's question — tap the pairs.
p: Arjuna's fear for the one who drifts off
is born again, and strives again
even a little of this dharma

s: in Hindu belief, a practice you drop is simply wasted
Krishna says no one who does good comes to a bad end; the effort carries on, even into a next life.
Arjuna told Krishna his mind is as hard to hold as the wind
and then asked what happens to the one who drifts off the path.
commentators all read 'no effort is lost' the same way
some read it generously, about any honest start; others about the yoga Krishna teaches.

games.q: you're Krishna. Arjuna asks: the one who started with faith and then wandered off, is he lost like a torn cloud? what do you say?
o: yes: unless you finish in this life, it's wasted.
no: no one who does good comes to a bad end; born again, they strive again.
it depends on how many years they practiced first.
games.why: Gita 6.40–43, in paraphrase: neither here nor hereafter are they destroyed. born again, they pick up the understanding they had, and strive again.

practice: Bring to mind one thing of your faith you once knew and let slip: a prayer, an aarti, a story, the habit of lighting a lamp. Don't scold yourself.
Say or hum the part you still remember, even one line, and let that be the next step, picked up where it was left.
If you pray, offer that line to God in your own way; if you don't, let one small practice from this year come back for a breath or two.

wordCard.voice: Year three. The great story, the saints and the teachers, walked, and, in the Gita's promise, kept.

orig.note: Sanskrit: svalpam apy asya dharmasya, 'even a little of this dharma,' from Bhagavad Gita 2.40.

carryVoice: Your line: no effort on the path is lost, even across lives. Krishna told Arjuna so. Year three, done.
